6. Final answer

Combining everything, we obtain that the initial value a1a_{1} can be exactly those numbers of the form

a1=6⋅12k⋅d(k∈ℕ0,d​odd, 5∤d).\boxed{a_{1}=6\cdot 12^{k}\cdot d\hskip 18.49988pt(k\in\mathbb{N}_{0},\;d\ \text{odd},\;5\nmid d).}

Equivalently, a1=22​k+1⋅3k+1⋅da_{1}=2^{2k+1}\cdot 3^{k+1}\cdot d with dd odd and not divisible by 55.

 

Model Proof
Notation and basic facts

Define Sn=∑i=1nxiS_{n}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i} and Qn=∑i=1nxi2Q_{n}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}^{2}.
The rules: on odd nn, Sn≤λ​nS_{n}\leq\lambda n; on even nn, Qn≤nQ_{n}\leq n.

From Cauchy-Schwarz, after any even turn 2​k2k we have

S2​k2≤(2​k)​Q2​k≤(2​k)⋅2​k=(2​k)2⟹S2​k≤2​k.S_{2k}^{2}\leq(2k)Q_{2k}\leq(2k)\cdot 2k=(2k)^{2}\hskip 9.24994pt\Longrightarrow\hskip 9.24994ptS_{2k}\leq 2k.

For k≥1k\geq 1 define the slack after the even turn 2​k2k:

dk=λ⁡(2​k+1)−S2​k.d_{k}=\lambda(2k+1)-S_{2k}.

Alice can move on turn 2​k+12k+1 iff dk≥0d_{k}\geq 0 (she may choose x2​k+1=0x_{2k+1}=0).

If at some odd turn Alice can legally choose a number u>2u>\sqrt{2} while Q2​k=2​kQ_{2k}=2k, then
Q2​k+1=2​k+u2>2​k+2Q_{2k+1}=2k+u^{2}>2k+2 and Bazza will have no legal move on the next turn, so Alice wins immediately.
In the general case, we will use the slack to analyse the game.

Key strategy for Bazza

We consider the following natural strategy for Bazza on even turns: after Alice’s move uu on turn 2​k+12k+1, if the game has not ended, Bazza chooses

v=2​k+2−Q2​k+1,v=\sqrt{2k+2-Q_{2k+1}},

i.e. the largest possible number that still satisfies Q2​k+2≤2​k+2Q_{2k+2}\leq 2k+2.
This choice is always legal as long as Q2​k+1≤2​k+2Q_{2k+1}\leq 2k+2 and makes Q2​k+2=2​k+2Q_{2k+2}=2k+2 (the maximal possible sum of squares).
We call this the maximal strategy for Bazza.

Claim 1. As long as Alice never picks a number u>2u>\sqrt{2} (which would make her win immediately), the maximal strategy forces Q2​k=2​kQ_{2k}=2k for every k≥1k\geq 1.

Proof. By induction. For k=1k=1, after Alice’s first move x1=ax_{1}=a (with 0≤a≤λ0\leq a\leq\lambda), Bazza can choose v=2−a2v=\sqrt{2-a^{2}} because a2≤2a^{2}\leq 2 (this holds for all relevant λ\lambda; in the cases where we apply it, we have λ≤2/2<2\lambda\leq\sqrt{2}/2<\sqrt{2}, and for larger λ\lambda Alice would win earlier). Then Q2=a2+v2=2Q_{2}=a^{2}+v^{2}=2. Inductive step: assume Q2​k=2​kQ_{2k}=2k. Alice’s move uu satisfies Q2​k+1=2​k+u2≤2​k+2Q_{2k+1}=2k+u^{2}\leq 2k+2 because otherwise u2>2u^{2}>2 and Alice would have won (this can only happen if Q2​k=2​kQ_{2k}=2k and u>2u>\sqrt{2}).D1††margin: If the game continues, we must have u≤2u\leq\sqrt{2}. Then Q2​k+1=2​k+u2≤2​k+2Q_{2k+1}=2k+u^{2}\leq 2k+2. Bazza chooses v=2​k+2−(2​k+u2)=2−u2v=\sqrt{2k+2-(2k+u^{2})}=\sqrt{2-u^{2}}, yielding Q2​k+2=2​k+2Q_{2k+2}=2k+2. □\square

Analysis of the slack under the maximal strategy

Suppose the maximal strategy is followed and that the game has not ended (so far Alice has never picked u>2u>\sqrt{2}). Let u=x2​k+1u=x_{2k+1} and v=x2​k+2v=x_{2k+2}. Then

S2​k+2=S2​k+u+v,Q2​k+2=2​k+2,S_{2k+2}=S_{2k}+u+v,\hskip 18.49988ptQ_{2k+2}=2k+2,

and therefore

dk+1=λ⁡(2​k+3)−S2​k+2=dk+2​λ−(u+v).d_{k+1}=\lambda(2k+3)-S_{2k+2}=d_{k}+2\lambda-(u+v).

For 0≤u≤20\leq u\leq\sqrt{2} define h⁡(u)=u+2−u2h(u)=u+\sqrt{2-u^{2}}. One checks that h⁡(u)≥2h(u)\geq\sqrt{2}, with equality exactly at u=0u=0 and u=2u=\sqrt{2}, and maximum 22 at u=1u=1. Consequently

dk+1≤dk+2​λ−2,d_{k+1}\leq d_{k}+2\lambda-\sqrt{2},

and equality can be achieved by choosing u=0u=0 (or u=2u=\sqrt{2}, if allowed).
Thus the maximal possible increase of dkd_{k} (when Alice tries to keep her slack large) is 2​λ−22\lambda-\sqrt{2}, attained by taking u=0u=0.

Three regimes

 

1. λ<22\lambda<\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}

Then 2​λ−2<02\lambda-\sqrt{2}<0.

Bazza’s winning strategy.
Bazza adopts the maximal strategy described above.

First, compute an upper bound for d1d_{1}. After the first two moves,
S2=a+2−a2S_{2}=a+\sqrt{2-a^{2}} with 0≤a≤λ0\leq a\leq\lambdaD2††margin: . The function f⁡(a)=a+2−a2f(a)=a+\sqrt{2-a^{2}} satisfies f⁡(a)≥2f(a)\geq\sqrt{2} (minimum at a=0a=0), so

d1=3​λ−S2≤3​λ−2.d_{1}=3\lambda-S_{2}\leq 3\lambda-\sqrt{2}.

Because λ<2/2\lambda<\sqrt{2}/2, we have 3​λ−2<2/2<23\lambda-\sqrt{2}<\sqrt{2}/2<\sqrt{2}.

Now, from (3) we obtain for any possible play

dk≤d1+(k−1)​(2​λ−2)≤(3​λ−2)+(k−1)​(2​λ−2).d_{k}\leq d_{1}+(k-1)(2\lambda-\sqrt{2})\leq(3\lambda-\sqrt{2})+(k-1)(2\lambda-\sqrt{2}).

(The first inequality follows by induction using dk+1≤dk+2​λ−2d_{k+1}\leq d_{k}+2\lambda-\sqrt{2}, the second uses the bound on d1d_{1}.)
Since 2​λ−2<02\lambda-\sqrt{2}<0, the right-hand side of (5) tends to −∞-\infty as k→∞k\to\infty. Hence there exists a finite KK with dK<0d_{K}<0.

When dK<0d_{K}<0, at the beginning of turn 2​K+12K+1 Alice cannot move (even x=0x=0 would violate the sum condition), so Bazza wins.

Moreover, we claim that Alice never gets the chance to win earlier by picking u>2u>\sqrt{2}. Indeed, from (5) and 2​λ−2<02\lambda-\sqrt{2}<0, we have dk≤3​λ−2<2d_{k}\leq 3\lambda-\sqrt{2}<\sqrt{2} for all kk. Hence dkd_{k} never exceeds 2\sqrt{2}, so she cannot legally pick a number larger than 2\sqrt{2} (which would be required to win immediately). Thus Bazza’s strategy is winning.

Conclusion for λ<2/2\lambda<\sqrt{2}/2: Bazza has a winning strategy.

 

2. λ=22\lambda=\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}

Here 2​λ−2=02\lambda-\sqrt{2}=0.

Bazza does not have a winning strategy.
We exhibit a strategy for Alice that prevents Bazza from ever winning.
Let Alice always choose x1=0x_{1}=0 and thereafter x2​k+1=0x_{2k+1}=0 on every odd turn.
Consider any Bazza moves. On even turns we have only Bazza’s numbers, say y1,…,yky_{1},\dots,y_{k} at turn 2​k2k. The constraints are ∑i=1kyi2=Q2​k≤2​k\sum_{i=1}^{k}y_{i}^{2}=Q_{2k}\leq 2k (because odd terms are zero). By Cauchy-Schwarz,

S2​k=∑i=1kyi≤k​∑i=1kyi2≤k⋅2​k=2​k.S_{2k}=\sum_{i=1}^{k}y_{i}\leq\sqrt{k\sum_{i=1}^{k}y_{i}^{2}}\leq\sqrt{k\cdot 2k}=\sqrt{2}\,k.

Therefore

dk=λ⁡(2​k+1)−S2​k≥22​(2​k+1)−2​k=22>0.d_{k}=\lambda(2k+1)-S_{2k}\geq\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(2k+1)-\sqrt{2}\,k=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}>0.

Thus Alice can always move (she may choose 00). Also, she never wins because to win she would need to make Q2​k+1>2​k+2Q_{2k+1}>2k+2, which would require x2​k+12>2​k+2−Q2​k≥2x_{2k+1}^{2}>2k+2-Q_{2k}\geq 2, i.e. x2​k+1>2x_{2k+1}>\sqrt{2}. But x2​k+1≤dkx_{2k+1}\leq d_{k} and we have not shown an upper bound on dkd_{k};D4††margin: however, the crucial point is that with this Alice strategy, Bazza never wins because Alice never loses. So this suffices to prove that Bazza does not have a winning strategy (he cannot force a win against every Alice strategy).

Alice does not have a winning strategy.
We now show that Bazza has a strategy to prevent Alice from winning.
Let Bazza adopt the maximal strategy (as in Case 1). We prove that under this strategy, Alice can never win.

First, by Claim 1, as long as the game continues, Q2​k=2​kQ_{2k}=2k. Using (3) with λ=2/2\lambda=\sqrt{2}/2 we get

dk+1=dk+2−(u+v)≤dk,d_{k+1}=d_{k}+\sqrt{2}-(u+v)\leq d_{k},

because u+v≥2u+v\geq\sqrt{2}. Hence dkd_{k} is non-increasing. Moreover, from (4) we have

d1≤3​λ−2=2/2.d_{1}\leq 3\lambda-\sqrt{2}=\sqrt{2}/2.

Thus dk≤2/2<2d_{k}\leq\sqrt{2}/2<\sqrt{2} for all kk. In particular, dkd_{k} never exceeds 2\sqrt{2}, so Alice can never pick a number u>2u>\sqrt{2} (which would be necessary to win immediately).

Could Alice win by picking some u≤2u\leq\sqrt{2} and later build up? To win, she must at some odd turn make Q2​k+1>2​k+2Q_{2k+1}>2k+2. Since Q2​k=2​kQ_{2k}=2k, this would require u2>2u^{2}>2, i.e. u>2u>\sqrt{2}. Thus any winning move would necessarily be u>2u>\sqrt{2}. Because dk≤2/2<2d_{k}\leq\sqrt{2}/2<\sqrt{2}, such a move is impossible. Therefore Alice never wins.D5††margin:

Additionally, we check that dkd_{k} never becomes negative, so Alice always can move. Indeed, using (2) and the fact that u≤dku\leq d_{k} (so u≤2/2<1u\leq\sqrt{2}/2<1), the smallest possible dk+1d_{k+1} for a given dkd_{k} is attained when u=dku=d_{k}, giving dk+1=2−2−dk2≥0d_{k+1}=\sqrt{2}-\sqrt{2-d_{k}^{2}}\geq 0. Hence dk≥0d_{k}\geq 0 for all kk.D6††margin:

Thus the maximal strategy by Bazza prevents Alice from winning, and also avoids his own loss (the game can continue indefinitely, e.g., if Alice always chooses 00, then dk=2/2d_{k}=\sqrt{2}/2 constant and Q2​k=2​kQ_{2k}=2k, so the play never ends). Consequently, Alice cannot force a win; she has no winning strategy.

Since neither player has a strategy that forces a win, the game is a draw for λ=2/2\lambda=\sqrt{2}/2.

 

3. λ>22\lambda>\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}

Now 2​λ−2>02\lambda-\sqrt{2}>0.

Alice’s winning strategy.
She will always choose 00 on her odd turns, until she can force a win.
Specifically, on turn 11 she sets x1=0x_{1}=0. On each subsequent odd turn 2​k+12k+1 (k≥1k\geq 1), she examines the current slack dk=λ⁡(2​k+1)−S2​kd_{k}=\lambda(2k+1)-S_{2k}. If dk>2​k+2−Q2​kd_{k}>\sqrt{2k+2-Q_{2k}}, she chooses a number uu with

2​k+2−Q2​k<u≤dk,\sqrt{2k+2-Q_{2k}}<u\leq d_{k},

such that u2>2​k+2−Q2​ku^{2}>2k+2-Q_{2k} (this is possible because dkd_{k} is strictly larger). She then wins on the next turn because Q2​k+1=Q2​k+u2>2​k+2Q_{2k+1}=Q_{2k}+u^{2}>2k+2. If dk≤2​k+2−Q2​kd_{k}\leq\sqrt{2k+2-Q_{2k}}, she simply chooses x2​k+1=0x_{2k+1}=0.

We must verify that this strategy is legal and that it indeed leads to a win.

First, note that as long as Alice always picks 00, all her moves contribute nothing to QQ and S2​kS_{2k} is the sum of Bazza’s even moves. For any Bazza strategy we have

Q2​k=∑i=1kx2​i2≤2​k,S2​k=∑i=1kx2​i.Q_{2k}=\sum_{i=1}^{k}x_{2i}^{2}\leq 2k,\hskip 18.49988ptS_{2k}=\sum_{i=1}^{k}x_{2i}.

By Cauchy-Schwarz,

S2​k2≤k​Q2​k≤2​k2⟹S2​k≤2​k.S_{2k}^{2}\leq k\,Q_{2k}\leq 2k^{2}\hskip 9.24994pt\Longrightarrow\hskip 9.24994ptS_{2k}\leq\sqrt{2}\,k.

Consequently,

dk=λ⁡(2​k+1)−S2​k≥λ⁡(2​k+1)−2​k=(2​λ−2)​k+λ.d_{k}=\lambda(2k+1)-S_{2k}\geq\lambda(2k+1)-\sqrt{2}\,k=(2\lambda-\sqrt{2})k+\lambda.

Because 2​λ−2>02\lambda-\sqrt{2}>0, the right-hand side of (8) tends to +∞+\infty as k→∞k\to\infty. In particular, there exists an integer KK such that

dK>2​K+2−Q2​K.d_{K}>\sqrt{2K+2-Q_{2K}}.

(Since the right side is at most 2​K+2\sqrt{2K+2}, it suffices that (2​λ−2)​K+λ>2​K+2(2\lambda-\sqrt{2})K+\lambda>\sqrt{2K+2}; this holds for all sufficiently large KK.)

At the start of turn 2​K+12K+1, we have dK>2​K+2−Q2​Kd_{K}>\sqrt{2K+2-Q_{2K}}. Choose

u=2​K+2−Q2​K+ε,u=\sqrt{2K+2-Q_{2K}}+\varepsilon,

with ε>0\varepsilon>0 small enough that u≤dKu\leq d_{K} (possible because dKd_{K} is strictly larger). Then

S2​K+1=S2​K+u≤S2​K+dK=λ⁡(2​K+1),S_{2K+1}=S_{2K}+u\leq S_{2K}+d_{K}=\lambda(2K+1),

so the sum condition is satisfied, and

Q2​K+1=Q2​K+u2>Q2​K+(2​K+2−Q2​K)=2​K+2.Q_{2K+1}=Q_{2K}+u^{2}>Q_{2K}+(2K+2-Q_{2K})=2K+2.

Therefore on turn 2​K+22K+2 Bazza has no legal move (even x=0x=0 would give Q>2​K+2Q>2K+2). Alice wins.

It remains to check that Alice can always make the choice x2​k+1=0x_{2k+1}=0 when dk≤2​k+2−Q2​kd_{k}\leq\sqrt{2k+2-Q_{2k}}. The condition for choosing 00 is that 0≤dk0\leq d_{k}, i.e. dk≥0d_{k}\geq 0. From (8), dk≥(2​λ−2)​k+λ>0d_{k}\geq(2\lambda-\sqrt{2})k+\lambda>0 for all kk (since the right side is positive for k=1k=1 because 3​λ−2>03\lambda-\sqrt{2}>0 for λ>2/2\lambda>\sqrt{2}/2). Hence Alice can always pick 00 when she does not want to win yet. Thus her strategy is well defined and guarantees a win in finite time.

Conclusion for λ>2/2\lambda>\sqrt{2}/2: Alice has a winning strategy.

 

Final answer

  • •

    Alice has a winning strategy iff λ>22\lambda>\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.

  • •

    Bazza has a winning strategy iff λ<22\lambda<\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.

  • •

    For λ=22\lambda=\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} neither player can force a win; the game can be drawn.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
